text: General elections were held in Argentina on 30 October 1983, marking the return of constitutional rule after the National Reorganization Process dictatorship began in 1976. Voters elected the president, governors, mayors, and their respective national, provincial, and municipal legislators, with a turnout of 85.6%. During 1976, the government of Isabel Perón faced severe crises, including violence from guerrilla groups like the Montoneros and the People's Revolutionary Army (ERP), which caused hundreds of deaths monthly, and the Argentine Anticommunist Alliance, which conducted counter-attacks using undercover agents. The Rodrigazo led to an annual inflation rate exceeding 600 percent, combined with union unrest that brought national industry to a virtual standstill. Congresswoman Cristina Guzmán accused Perón of misusing charity funds, but Congress refused to impeach her. These conditions contributed to the 1976 military coup, as most of society viewed the military as the only viable solution. General Roberto Viola was removed in 1981 by Leopoldo Galtieri in a "palace coup," which increased the Argentine Navy's political influence. Opposed by other military factions and fearing removal, Galtieri planned an invasion of the Falkland Islands. The 1982 invasion boosted the military junta's popularity but triggered a bank panic and undermined Minister Roberto Alemann's efforts to reduce inflation and stabilize the economy. After Argentina's surrender in the Falklands War, public support sharply declined, especially due to media distortion and the surprise nature of the defeat. Six years of wage freezes, industry-unfriendly policies, and restrictive measures such as Circular 1050 had reduced GDP per capita to its lowest level since 1968 and lowered real wages by about 40%. The restoration of freedoms sparked widespread strikes, including two led by Saúl Ubaldini of the CGT labor federation, the largest in South America. This heightened tensions among hard-liners, prompting Admiral Jorge Anaya—later court-martialed for gross malfeasance in the 1982 Falklands War—to announce his presidential candidacy in August, becoming the first to do so; Bignone immediately blocked the move. In response to growing demands for elections, police violently suppressed a December 16, 1982, demonstration in Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo, killing one protester and ending Bignone's hopes for delaying elections indefinitely. To manage the crisis, the regime began destroying evidence of the murder of between 15,000 and 30,000 dissidents—mostly students, academics, and labor union members—during the 1973–1976 period. In February 1983, Buenos Aires Police Chief Ramón Camps publicly acknowledged the crime, stating the "disappeared" were dead, which provoked public outrage and forced President Bignone to stop denying the tragedy. On April 28, he declared a blanket amnesty for those involved, including himself. Among the first to condemn the amnesty was Raúl Alfonsín, leader of the UCR's progressive wing, who won his party's nomination at a July convention. He chose Víctor Martínez, a more conservative UCR figure from Córdoba Province, as his running mate. The Justicialist Party struggled to select candidates, both for the presidential ticket and key local races, as its left wing—targeted during repression before and after the 1976 coup—was weak due to the CGT's influence. They nominated Ítalo Luder, who had served as acting president during Isabel Perón's 1975 illness and authorized repression against the left, and Deolindo Bittel, a populist known for defending Habeas Corpus during the dictatorship, as their presidential and vice-presidential candidates, respectively. Alfonsín focused his campaign on accusing the Justicialists of tacitly supporting Bignone's amnesty. He gained strong backing from Argentine intellectuals and artists, including playwright Carlos Gorostiza, who created the slogan "Ahora, Alfonsín" ("Now is the Time for Alfonsín"). Luder limited his campaign to references of Juan Perón, and polls showed no clear lead. A few days before the October 30 election, Justicialist candidate Herminio Iglesias held a premature "victory rally" in which a coffin draped in UCR colors was burned on television. The bonfire stirred painful memories of Isabel Perón's rule and contributed to a decisive victory for the UCR. The Peronists won a majority in the Senate and 12 of 22 governorships, while the UCR secured only 7 governors, though Buenos Aires Province was led by UCR's Alejandro Armendáriz. Alfonsín persuaded Bignone to move the inauguration to December 10, 1983. The Alfonsín–Martínez ticket won with 52% of the vote, defeating the Luder–Bittel ticket, which received 40%. Alfonsín's 52% vote share was later surpassed by Cristina Fernández de Kirchner's 54% in 2011.
